lesson.title: Slicing Lists: Grabbing a Chunk Without a Loop
lesson.summary: Using the start:stop:step syntax to pull out a whole sub-list at once, and why every slice hands you back a brand new list.
lesson.body:
Indexing gets you one element at a time. Often you want a range of elements instead, the first three scores, everything after the header row, every other item. Rather than writing a loop to collect those elements one by one, Python lets you describe the whole range in a single expression called a slice, using the same square brackets you already know from string slicing and list indexing, but now with a colon inside.

The full slice syntax is my_list[start:stop:step]. start is the index where the slice begins, stop is the index where it ends, and stop is always exclusive, meaning the element at that index is not included. step controls how many positions to move forward between each included element, and it defaults to 1 if you leave it out. Any of the three parts can be omitted: leaving out start means "begin at the very front," leaving out stop means "continue to the very end," and leaving out step keeps the default of moving one element at a time.

nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
print(nums[1:4])
print(nums[:3])
print(nums[3:])
print(nums[-3:])
print(nums[::2])
print(nums[::-1])

Trace each line against the indices of nums, which run 0 through 5 for values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. nums[1:4] starts at index 1 and stops before index 4, grabbing indices 1, 2, and 3, which is [20, 30, 40]. nums[:3] starts at the front and stops before index 3, grabbing indices 0, 1, 2, which is [10, 20, 30]. nums[3:] starts at index 3 and runs to the end, grabbing indices 3, 4, 5, which is [40, 50, 60]. nums[-3:] counts three from the end and takes everything from there onward, which lands on the same indices 3, 4, 5, giving [40, 50, 60] again. nums[::2] takes every second element starting from the front, indices 0, 2, 4, giving [10, 30, 50]. Finally nums[::-1] uses a step of negative one, walking backward through the whole list, which reverses it entirely into [60, 50, 40, 30, 20, 10].

Unlike indexing a single element, slicing is forgiving about out-of-range boundaries. Asking for nums[2:100] does not raise an IndexError the way nums[100] would; Python simply stops at whatever elements actually exist and returns [30, 40, 50, 60]. This makes slicing a safe way to say "give me up to this many elements" without first checking how long the list actually is.

One detail matters more than any other for the concepts coming up: a slice always produces a brand new list object, a shallow copy of the selected elements, never the original list itself. If you write recent = nums[3:], recent is an entirely separate list in memory that happens to start out with the same values as the tail of nums. Changing recent afterward will not touch nums at all, and this is precisely the tool you will lean on in the next concept to make safe copies of a list before modifying it, sidestepping the aliasing problems that come from mutability.
